trace.claim: The paper asks whether stigmatizing Democratic campaign labels applied to Trump spill over to worsen Democrats’ perceptions of people with criminal records and how representation perceptions are affected.

Exposure to the Democratic Trump ad labeling him a convicted criminal negatively shifts Democrats’ perceptions of people with criminal records but improves perceived representation, and a counter-stereotype narrative largely mitigates the negative perceptual effects.
The study uses a three-arm online survey experiment with Democrats recruited via Prolific.
The Trump advertisement alone significantly reduced positive perceptions of individuals with criminal records relative to no exposure.
The counter-narrative presented before the ad greatly reduced support for the ad and improved perceptions of people with records.
Exposure to the Trump ad improved perceived feelings of representation among Democrats.
The counter-narrative decreased perceived quality of Democratic representation relative to the ad alone.
The authors note the study is preliminary and call for well-powered field experiments to confirm and extend findings.
The design cannot isolate the effect of the counter-narrative alone because it was always paired with the ad.
The paper is positioned within social categorization theory, using it to explain spillover of stigmatizing labels.
Prior literature is cited as claiming negative campaign advertisements help election success, which the authors dispute.
